title: Context Object Smuggling (AppContext Injection)
pattern: Creating a generic container struct holding all environment parameters and credentials, and passing a reference to it (`&AppContext`) down to almost every function in the application hierarchy.
why_bad: Violates interface specificity and information hiding. A function's signature no longer documents what it actually reads or writes. Any change to the global `AppContext` forces a recompilation of every calling module. It also makes isolated unit testing highly painful, as developers must construct a full mock `AppContext` (including unrelated API keys) just to test a simple database write.
detection: Observe a broad, flat context struct being passed as a parameter to more than 80% of the functions across multiple distinct modules, especially when those functions only access a single field of the context.
counterexample: `Context-dependent`. Web frameworks that inject a standard request-scoped state object at the controller entry point, where framework constraints require a uniform signature.
fix: Pass only the specific, individual dependencies that the function actually needs to perform its work.
source: *John K. Ousterhout - A Philosophy of Software Design (2018)*, Chapter 8, "Shared Variables" (Context Objects); *Robert C. Martin - Clean Code (2008)*, Chapter 3.
